 Skin Care 
 I’m a guy turning 42. This is how I just revamped my skin care routine
 By Henry T. Casey , CNN Underscored
 Published
 9:29 AM EDT, Sun October 25, 2026
 Link Copied!
 Henry T. Casey/CNN Underscored 
 In this article 
 Cleanser 
 Serum 
 Eye cream 
 Moisturizer 
 Sunscreen 
 Bottom line 
 FAQs 
 Meet our expert 
 Why trust CNN Underscored 
 This summer, back when I was a few months away from my imminent 42nd birthday, I was looking in the mirror and realized it was time to get my skin care routine back in working order. As many of my peers know, this is the decade when even guys start thinking about maintaining healthy skin as we notice certain signs of aging — which became all the more clear at the end of my first two months of the new routine I’ve been testing. As someone who appears on camera for CNN Underscored and loves to post a selfie with a fresh haircut or outfit, I’m willing to admit that my looks are important, even though I stopped keeping up my former routine somewhere around a year or so ago.
 To restart my skin care journey, I consulted CNN Underscored’s fashion and beauty editor Sophie Shaw , who came up with a whole routine for me, complete with a day and night regimen. She factored in my skin type and age, choosing products that are helpful for maturing skin as well as nonnegotiables like face moisturizer and sunscreen. I carefully started to add each item into my routine one at a time, with a couple of days in between each so I could tell which product (if any) resulted in an adverse reaction.
 In order to feel informed enough to make these good habits actually stick, I sought out advice from Dr. Jacob Beer , a board-certified dermatologist at Beer Dermatology . He cleared up my main confusion about consistency, telling me that “there’s such a marginal difference” between my perfectionist’s attitude that I need to be doing a daily routine and the five-days-and-nights per week schedule I typically rock. He just warned about the overall “trap” where patients start saying “’I don’t have to do this every night’ and take off two days a week, then three days a week and then it just goes down from there.”
 Henry T. Casey/CNN Underscored 
 Aside from the acne-prone, pimply teenage years, my skin’s been pretty good over the years, but around four years ago I decided to start taking better care of it per a close friend’s warning that aging was coming for me. When I’ve been good about my routine, everything’s been easy. When I’ve been lazy, well, there have been small reddish blemishes (more on those later), and I’ve also had to keep a supply of pimple patches on hand.
 One last thing before we get into the results of my testing: The pronounced lines in my forehead are long-time residents on my visage, from a childhood accident, and not the wrinkles that some of these products are meant to erase. So, those lines aside, I evaluated how well the new routine worked and what steps seemed to make the biggest difference in other areas of my complexion. Here’s everything I learned while testing 10 skin care products on the precipice of 42.
 Cleanser
 CosRX Low-pH Good Morning Gel Face Cleanser 
 COSRX Low pH Good Morning Gel Cleanser, Daily Mild Face Cleanser for Sensitive Skin with BHA & Tea-Tree Oil, PH Balancing, Korean Skin Care (5.07fl.oz/150ml) 
 Amazon 
 This mild face cleanser offers a foaming action and is great for starting the day off on a neutral level.
 $14 
 $10 at Amazon
 $12 at Walmart
 $14 at Ulta Beauty
 $14 at Nordstrom
 Henry T. Casey/CNN Underscored 
 The CosRX cleanser is the only skin care product in this routine that I’d consistently used in the weeks prior to this round of testing, and I’ve stuck with it for good reasons. It leaves my face feeling and looking clean without any negative reaction, and it foams with minimal effort and doesn’t require me to use much of the gel, too. The low-pH in the product’s name indicates that it’s mildly acidic, which is compatible with the skin’s natural baseline pH of about 5.5 , which leans naturally acidic too. This means that it’s gentle on the skin. It’s also sold in drug stores and specialty skin care stores near me, so I don’t even need to think about another online order.
 What I liked about it: The perfect wake-up, it left my skin looking and feeling neutral, and ready for all the layers to come.
 What I didn’t like about it: Absolutely nothing. I will keep using this as long as they make it.
 EltaMD Oil-in-Gel Cleanser 
 Amazon 
 You massage this cleanser into your face dry, then it turns into a milky emulsion as you rinse it off your face.
 $39 at Amazon
 $39 at Walmart
 $39 at Dermstore
 $39 at Bluemercury
 While I’m not entirely new to the skin care game, oil-in-gel cleansers are completely new to me. If you’re just as uninitiated as I was, this is first step at the end of the day because it gently removes all the sunscreen and product that’s still on your face. According to Shaw, it combines what could be two separate steps — an oil cleanse and a water-based face wash — into one easy rinse. It’s definitely a surprising product to use, as rubbing the oily gel into my face felt a bit disarming, and getting the milky white results as I washed it off was a surprise the first time. I’ve since come to really enjoy it because of how I’ve actually seen (or think I’ve seen) it remove impurities with small black specks coming out during the wash.
 What I liked about it: I love how it brings my skin back to where it was that morning.
 What I didn’t like about it: It’s harder to gauge how much you need to use than foaming cleansers, and I had to order it online.
 Serum
 Best Tested 
 The Ordinary Anti-Aging Peptide Serum 
 Sephora 
 This serum hydrates skin while fighting to smooth out and erase lines and wrinkles.
 Read our review 
 $20 
 $16 at Amazon
 From $20 at Sephora
 From $20 at The Ordinary
 $20 at Ulta Beauty
 I’ve heard a lot about peptides , and I’ve frankly ignored most of it (especially because of all of the black market options I see advertised), but I was open to testing The Ordinary’s own multi-peptide and hyaluronic acid serum, since some of the most trustworthy people I know about skin care talk about this company as one of the standard-bearers of the moment. It’s also worth noting we named it one of the best hydrating serums , and I did find that it kept my skin comfortable without feeling heavy or greasy. On top of it’s moisturizing properties, the peptides are supposed to help smooth fine lines and wrinkles. While I don’t think I have the kinds of wrinkles it’s targeting, my skin does look and feel a little smoother and firmer.
 What I liked about it: The absolutely easiest application: its eye-dropper was big enough to use without fidgeting and the serum easily blended into my skin. The price feels exactly right for what you get for this $20 bottle.
 What I didn’t like about it: I’m not exactly at a point with my overall face wrinkles where I’m seeing the most bang for my buck here.
 Sophie Shaw/CNN Underscored 
 Related article 
 The Ordinary’s skin care is cheap, but is it good? I put 15 bestsellers to the test 
 Sunday Riley C.E.O. 15% Vitamin C Brightening Serum 
 Sephora 
 Designed to breathe life back into your skin, this serum brightens and evens skin tone with 15% vitamin C. It's a daytime product, so I applied this in the morning.
 From $43 at Dermstore
 From $50 at Sephora
 From $50 at Ulta Beauty
 From $85 at Nordstrom
 Henry T. Casey/CNN Underscored 
 When I talked to Beer about what to expect from a vitamin C serum, he informed me that I should see a “subtle brightening” after my two months of testing, and he was right on the money. I never thought of my skin as dull, mostly because I never thought of the bounce or luminosity of my face’s skin (and I never thought I’d say anything positive about a C.E.O. either), but Sunday Riley’s C.E.O. Vitamin C Brightening Serum is changing my tone, literally. Yes, as you can see in the before and after in the Bottom Line section of this story, one of the biggest, most notable changes is how an overall redness that I’m not a fan of is gone and replaced with a much more even, natural skin tone. I also appreciate that the pump bottle locks and fits in my dopp kit while traveling.
 What I liked about it: The serum quickly disappeared into my skin with rapid absorption, helping me get to the sunscreen stage of the routine quicker. More importantly, it showed results.
 What I didn’t like about it: This one is a bit more expensive than I’d like, at $85 for a one-ounce bottle.
 Medik8 Crystal Retinal 6 Serum 
 Medik8 Crystal Retinal 6 - Brightening, Firming, Advanced Skin Retinaldehyde Serum - Smooths Wrinkles - Hyaluronic Acid, Glycerin, Vitamin E - 1 oz 
 Amazon.com 
 This over-the-counter retinal is an overall anti-aging face serum that improves skin tone and fights wrinkles overnight.
 $87 at Amazon
 $87 at Dermstore
 Henry T. Casey/CNN Underscored 
 In terms of ease-of-use, the Medik8 Crystal Retinal 6 is a huge step up from my previous retinol, Sunday Riley’s Luna Face Oil , which is a liquid that you eye-drop onto your face, and seemed to just run in whatever direction it felt like. Instead, Retinal 6 is a creamy consistency that I massaged into my face five nights a week. Retinol and retinal live within the vitamin A derivative family, which are considered some of the best anti-aging ingredients . The product comes in six different strengths, and the Retinal 6 is a middle- of-the-pack option — it’s considered best for “regular vitamin A users” according to the brand, not for retinol novices but not a super high potency, either. While retinol is known for causing irritation or skin sensitivity, I had zero negative reaction. It shares points with the Sunday Riley Good Genes Lactic Acid for the reduction of small red blemishes and the Sunday Riley C.E.O. for the overall tone brightening.
 What I liked about it: Smooth application and easier to cover my whole face than the retinol face oil I was previously using. I didn’t have any negative reaction — like dryness or flaking — that is commonly associated with retinol.
 What I didn’t like about it: $87 per ounce is a little heavy.
 Sunday Riley Good Genes All-in-One Lactic Acid Treatment 
 Amazon 
 This lactic acid is designed to exfoliate your complexion , helping to even out skin texture, unclog pores and brighten the skin. 
 From $50 at Amazon
 From $50 at Nordstrom
 From $50 at Sephora
 From $50 at Ulta Beauty
 Henry T. Casey/CNN Underscored 
 I was familiar with Good Genes, but my testing restored my faith after taking a lot of time off from using it because — to be frank — I got cheap. It’s actually one of my lowkey winners of the pack. With a mere two applications per week — on the nights I did not apply the Medik8 retinol — this lactic acid did wonders for knocking out some of the blemishes under my eyes. It also has the best and worst aspects of the pump bottle design that I saw with Medik8 Crystal Retinal 6 and Sunday Riley C.E.O.: It’s got a neat design that’s easy to use but when it runs low you’re really at the mercy of where its pump is sitting. Yes, folks who are more used to beauty products probably are rolling their eyes, but as someone still in his early days, I yearn for an easier way to get every last drop out of this $85 container.
 What I liked about it: It clarified my skin in places that actually impressed me.
 What I didn’t like about it: Again, one fluid ounce is $85, which kind of irritates me more than those red blemishes it removed.
 Sophie Shaw/CNN Underscored 
 Related article 
 We consulted 11 skin care experts to find the best face serums for wrinkles, acne and more 
 Eye cream
 The Inkey List Caffeine Eye Cream 
 Sephora 
 The Inkey List claims you’ll get the best results by using this eye cream after keeping it in your fridge for a depuffing effect.
 $14 at Amazon
 $14 at Sephora
 $14 at The Inkey List
 Henry T. Casey/CNN Underscored 
 As someone who’s nearly always caffeinated , this $14 tube of eye cream caught my eye with its name, as well as the fact that you’re supposed to keep it in the fridge to enhance its cooling and depuffing qualities . Fortunately for me, though, I’ve never had a problem with puffy eyes and bagginess. That said, it did give a refreshing kick in my morning routine. And I give this eye cream points for reducing the amount of pronounced lines in my eyelid area and by my nose. My only real frustration comes with how the tiny tube makes it difficult to get the right amount of product out. I only needed a teeny tiny amount of the cream, and it was kinda difficult to be that precise. I had some minor eye irritation at random parts of the day, often in the afternoon, and I always wondered if it was because of excessive eye cream.
 What I liked about it: This blended in smoothly and the cool sensation in the mornings was a nice touch. I even saw some line and wrinkle fighting.
 What I didn’t like about it: You need a really fine touch to only extract the small amount you need.
 Clinique Clinical Repair Wrinkle Correcting Anti-Aging Eye Cream 
 Sephora 
 This easy-to-apply eye cream fights wrinkles and puffiness with hydrating ingredients and peptides.
 From $66 at Amazon
 From $66 at Bloomingdale's
 From $66 at Ulta Beauty
 $66 at Sephora
 Eye cream is one of those things that always feels a little like extra-credit, but since the lines between my eyes and my nose have been reduced, I can confidently say that what I did worked. That said, since I also used The Inkey’s eye cream, there’s a question of which actually did the work. Based on the ingredients list, Clinique’s formula is more geared towards treating lines and wrinkles with a bunch of peptides. It could also just be the fact that I’m showing that area some extra TLC and hydration with the eye creams two times a day now (The Inkey List in the morning and Clinique at night).
 Once my testing samples run out, I might just replenish the Clinique, and see if the affected area stays as it is now. If the lines near my eyes and nose come back, I’ll probably switch to The Inkey List eye cream to see if that does the trick.
 What I liked about it: This eye cream reduced my eye wrinkles and was much easier to use than The Inkey List.
 What I didn’t like about it: The $100 for an ounce raises the hair on my arms ever so slightly.
 Moisturizer
 Native Facial Moisturizer 
 Amazon 
 This moisturizer is sold in hydrating and gentle versions , and the latter is made for sensitive skin.
 $15 
 $14 at Amazon
 $15 at Walmart
 Henry T. Casey/CNN Underscored 
 It took me a while to actually “like” Native’s moisturizer because its design isn’t quite what I’d call tired brain-friendly — and as a part of my nighttime routine I needed something low-effort. A full pump of its dispenser leaves me with far more moisturizer than my face needs, and applying all of it leaves some bits unabsorbed and caked on top of my face. Once I figured out the precise amount of push needed, I found myself with no extra residue and a perfectly moist face. I didn’t notice a difference between the Hydrating and Gentle versions, but those with sensitive skin may prefer the latter’s fragrance-free formula.
 What I liked about it: When I woke up in the morning, I noticed I was still moisturized, so it did its job to the fullest.
 What I didn’t like about it: It took me a while to learn how you only need to give a light, short press to get enough product. Despite it being a drugstore brand, it was oddly tough to find this product in a store near me.
 Molly Flores/CNN Underscored 
 Related article 
 The best face moisturizers in 2026 for every skin type, tested and reviewed 
 Sunscreen
 Beauty of Joseon Dayscreen Moisturizer SPF 30 
 Sephora 
 This lightweight sunscreen also works as your daytime moisturizer, thanks to Beauty of Joseon’s Green Tea-HA ingredient that uses antioxidants as it hydrates.
 $20 at Amazon
 $20 at Sephora
 Henry T. Casey/CNN Underscored 
 As a fan of Beauty of Joseon’s moisturizing Relief Sun Aqua-Fresh Rice + B5 sunscreen , I didn’t know what to expect from the company’s Dayscreen formula. After two months of testing, I think I’ve found my new sunscreen, because it’s got a lighter consistency than the Relief Sun version, and shows even fewer (actually, zero) signs of it being there at all. I didn’t have any issues with the reduction in SPF intensity, either, going from SPF 50 in the Relief Sun to the Dayscreen’s SPF 30, though I was nearly perfect about following the “every two hours” reapplication instructions.
 What I liked about it: It provides protection from the sun and doubles as moisturizer, so I didn’t need to apply another layer in my morning routine.
 What I didn’t like about it: Absolutely nothing! Another of the flawless products I tested.
 Sophie Shaw/CNN Underscored 
 Related article 
 17 best Korean sunscreens, according to dermatologists and K-beauty lovers 
 Bottom line
 Henry T. Casey/CNN Underscored 
 Henry T. Casey/CNN Underscored 
 Looking at the before and after, I’m relatively pleased with the results of this testing, and I want to keep this skin care routine going for now. That said, I am sure that simplifying the number of products and beauty brands will ensure continued consistency, which is what I know I need. In the later weeks of this testing, I was struggling with an unrelated illness that made keeping this routine going annoying but not impossible.
 So, while I know I’ll keep using both the CosRX and EltaMD cleansers , I think I’ll probably stick with just the Clinique eye cream once the other Inkey List tube runs out, since it’s a little harder to use. As for the rest of my routine, I’ll keep alternating between Beauty of Joseon Dayscreen and Native Facial Moisturizer for day and night applications, and The Ordinary’s Multi-Peptide + HA serum is sticking around as well.
 What I’m less sure about is the pricier trio of C.E.O., Good Genes and Crystal Retinal 6. Using all of them relatively simultaneously has worked wonders, but they combine to $257 total for an ounce of each. I think I care about the skin tone vibrancy that C.E.O. helped with the most, but I know your mileage may vary. If anyone asks for my personal recommendation, I’m going to tell them to start with the cleanser and sunscreen, and then make that habit work before finding other things to add on.
 FAQs
 Should a 40-year-old use retinol?
 If you’re looking for general long-term care, it’s a good idea. Beer told me that he considers retinols “more for maintenance.” He also noted that you will need “six to eight weeks, even with prescription strength” versions to see any differences or changes.
 What are the best skin care products for people in their 40s?
 Beer recommends a “minimum package of a cleanser, a moisturizer and then a sunscreen,” to men in their 40s, “whichever ones of those you can tolerate will help decrease fine lines and wrinkles later on.”
 What other reasons are there for using skin care products?
 Beer advises patients that skin care isn’t just about aesthetics, saying that “in some cases also using things like sunscreen, especially, but even tretinoin or retinoids in certain cases, can decrease the prevalence of getting cancer later on.”
 Meet our expert
 For this article, we consulted the following expert to gain his professional insights on skin care advice for men in their 40s:
 Dr. Jacob Beer , board-certified dermatologist at Beer Dermatology 
 Why trust CNN Underscored
 CNN Underscored editors and writers ensure every product included in an article is thoroughly vetted and something we ourselves would feel comfortable buying and using. Our team has many decades of collective experience researching, testing and recommending products across every category — from fashion and food, to home goods and health, to electronics and everything in between — and we’re committed to using that expertise to help you make the most of your money and live a better life.
 For this article, CNN Underscored tech writer Henry T. Casey spent over two months testing this battery of skin care products. He’s hoping that consistent use of at least a cleanser, sunscreen and moisturizer will ensure he never even needs to really understand why red light therapy masks exist.
